Law of Christ
law uv kryst
noun phrase (Galatians 6:2)
From the apostle's phrase “the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2) and “under the law to Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21); the rule of life that binds the believer under the lordship of Christ.

Biblical Definition

The law of Christ is the rule of life that binds the believer under the lordship of Christ—the moral will of God as it comes to His people in and through their Redeemer. Paul names it directly: “Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ”; and he describes himself as “not without law to God, but under the law to Christ.” The phrase guards two truths against distortion. First, the believer is not lawless: though delivered from the law as a covenant of works and from the ceremonial yoke, he is not without law to God but bound to the abiding moral law, now established and deepened by Christ. The Lord summed it in the new commandment, “that ye love one another; as I have loved you”—not a lower standard than the old law but a higher, for love is the fulfilling of the law. Second, this obedience flows from a new principle: “the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death.” The believer keeps the law not as a slave earning wages, but as a son walking in the Spirit, with the law written on the heart of flesh. The dictionary marks the law of Christ against two errors. The antinomian seizes the phrase to abolish all law, as though grace freed the believer from the moral commands of God; but Christ came to establish the law, not to destroy it, and His law binds. The legalist, on the other side, would drag the believer back under the law as a covenant of works or under the ceremonial yoke; but the believer is under the law to Christ, kept by grace, fulfilling it by love and the Spirit. The law of Christ is neither lawlessness nor bondage, but the glad obedience of the free son of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

The rule of life binding the believer under Christ's lordship (Galatians 6:2; 1 Corinthians 9:21)—the abiding moral law established and deepened by Christ, fulfilled by love and the Spirit; against both antinomian lawlessness and legalist bondage.

LAW OF CHRIST, noun phrase. The rule of life binding the believer under the lordship of Christ.

“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).

The believer is “under the law to Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21)—not lawless.

Summed in the new commandment to love as Christ loved (John 13:34).

Kept by the law of the Spirit of life, not as a slave but a son (Romans 8:2).

Key Scripture

Ga 6:2 — "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ."

1 Co 9:21 — "To them that are without law, as without law, (being not without law to God, but under the law to Christ,) that I might gain them that are without law."

Joh 13:34 — "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another."

Ro 8:2 — "For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death."

Modern Corruption

The antinomian seizes “law of Christ” to abolish all law; the legalist drags the believer back under the law as a covenant of works or the ceremonial yoke. Both miss the glad obedience of the free son.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is obedience under grace—neither lawless nor enslaved. The antinomian seizes the phrase “law of Christ” to abolish all law, reasoning that grace has freed the believer from the moral commands of God, so that holiness is optional and the commandments passed away with the old covenant. The dictionary answers that the believer is “not without law to God, but under the law to Christ.” Christ came not to destroy the moral law but to establish and deepen it; His new commandment of love is no lower standard than the old but a higher, for love is the fulfilling of the law. The free son is bound to obey.

The legalist commits the opposite error, dragging the believer back under the law as a covenant of works to be kept for acceptance, or under the ceremonial yoke the gospel removed. But the believer keeps the law of Christ not as a slave earning wages but as a son walking in the Spirit, the law of the Spirit of life having freed him from the law of sin and death, the moral law written on his heart of flesh. The dictionary holds the balance: the law of Christ is neither the antinomian's lawlessness nor the legalist's bondage, but the glad, Spirit-wrought, love-fulfilled obedience of those whom grace has made free and sons.

Hebrew Roots

From the Greek nomos tou Christou (“law of Christ,” Galatians 6:2) and ennomos Christou (“under the law to Christ,” 1 Corinthians 9:21); the moral law as it binds the believer under his Redeemer.

Nomos tou Christou, Greek, “the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).

Ennomos Christou, Greek, “under the law to Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21).

The new commandment of love (John 13:34), the law's fulfilling.

“The law of the Spirit of life” that frees from sin and death (Romans 8:2).

Neither antinomian lawlessness nor legalist bondage, but filial obedience.

Usage

"The pastor preached the law of Christ to answer the antinomian: the free son is bound to obey."

"He showed the believer under the law to Christ, kept not as a slave but as a son in the Spirit."

"She fulfilled the law of Christ by bearing her brethren's burdens in love."
